e.etymology: The French form of Latin Marcellus, a diminutive of Marcus, a Roman name linked to Mars, the god of war.
namesakes: Marcel Proust (French novelist)
Marcel Marceau (French mime)
Marcel the Shell (stop-motion film character)

assoc.t: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On, stop-motion film star
Marcel, Ross's pet monkey on Friends

e.etymology: A form of the biblical Azariah, Hebrew Azaryah, 'God has helped', a name borne by many men in the Old Testament. In the US this spelling is given mostly to girls.
From Spanish dulce, 'sweet', from Latin dulcis. It began as a short form of religious names such as Dulce Nombre de Maria, 'sweet name of Mary'.

assoc.t: dulce, Spanish for sweet or candy
dulce de leche, caramel-like milk sweet

e.etymology: The form of Thomas used in Spanish (written Tomás), Czech, Lithuanian and Swedish, from Aramaic te'oma, 'twin', the byname of one of the twelve apostles.
From an English surname taken from Axton in Kent, Old English for 'Acca's stone'. It caught on in the US in the 2010s beside Paxton, Jaxton and Axel.
From Old Norse Hlif, 'protection', now identified with the Scandinavian word liv, 'life'. In Norse myth Lif is the woman who survives Ragnarok. In English it is also short for Olivia.
namesakes: Liv Tyler (actress, The Lord of the Rings)
Liv Ullmann (Norwegian actress)
Liv Rooney (twin in Disney Channel's Liv and Maddie)

assoc.t: LIV Golf, Saudi-backed professional golf league

e.etymology: From an occupational surname, Middle English gage: either 'measure', for an assayer, or 'pledge', for a moneylender. It rose as a first name in the 1990s, after the toddler Gage in the 1989 film Pet Sematary.

assoc.t: gauge, the measuring instrument (same sound)

e.etymology: From Belén, the Spanish name of Bethlehem, the birthplace of Jesus, from Hebrew bet lechem, 'house of bread'. It is also the Spanish word for a nativity scene.
From the Latin saint's name Ambrosius, from Greek ambrosios, 'immortal, divine', the word behind ambrosia. Saint Ambrose was the 4th-century bishop of Milan who baptized Augustine.
namesakes: Saint Ambrose (4th-century bishop of Milan)
Ambrose Bierce (author of The Devil's Dictionary)
Ambrose Burnside (Civil War general, namesake of sideburns)

e.etymology: A short form of Indiana, India and Indigo, now given on its own. Indy is also the nickname of Indiana Jones and of the city of Indianapolis.

assoc.t: Indy, nickname of the film hero Indiana Jones
Indy, nickname of Indianapolis and its 500-mile race
indie, short for independent music and film

e.etymology: From the River Clyde, which runs through Glasgow; the river's name is Celtic and of uncertain meaning. It became a first name in the 19th century, especially in the United States.
namesakes: Clyde Barrow (outlaw of Bonnie and Clyde)
Clyde Drexler (NBA Hall of Famer)

assoc.t: Clyde Barrow of the outlaw duo Bonnie and Clyde
Clyde, the orange ghost in Pac-Man

e.etymology: From an occupational surname for a wagon maker or driver, Old English waegn, 'wagon'. John Wayne's fame helped carry it to its US peak in the 1940s.
namesakes: Wayne Gretzky (hockey legend known as The Great One)
Wayne Newton (Las Vegas entertainer)
Wayne Brady (comedian and TV host)

assoc.t: Bruce Wayne, Batman's alter ego
John Wayne, Western film star
Wayne's World, SNL sketch and 1992 film
Lil Wayne, rapper

e.etymology: From the gem, one of the jewel names that came into fashion in the late 19th century. It also served as an English form of the Yiddish name Perle and as a pet form of Margaret, which means 'pearl'.
namesakes: Pearl Bailey (singer and actress)
Pearl S. Buck (Nobel-winning author of The Good Earth)
Pearl (Hester Prynne's daughter in The Scarlet Letter)

assoc.t: pearl, the gem and June birthstone
Pearl Krabs, the whale daughter in SpongeBob

e.etymology: A Spanish blend of Maria and Soledad, from the Marian title Our Lady of Solitude. It is also read as Maria del Sol, or as mar y sol, 'sea and sun'.
From Spanish and Portuguese salvador, 'savior', a name honoring Jesus Christ, from Latin salvator.
namesakes: Salvador Dalí (Spanish surrealist painter)

assoc.t: El Salvador, Central American country
Salvador Dalí, surrealist painter

e.etymology: A modern name used mainly in African American families. Name books give it as West African, 'kingly', but no source language has been documented.
The feminine of Ramon, the Spanish form of Raymond, from Germanic ragin, 'counsel', and mund, 'protection'. Helen Hunt Jackson's 1884 novel Ramona made it popular in the US.
namesakes: Ramona Quimby (heroine of Beverly Cleary's children's books)
Ramona Flowers (love interest in Scott Pilgrim vs. the World)
Ramona Singer (The Real Housewives of New York City)

assoc.t: Ramona Quimby, Beverly Cleary's spirited heroine

e.etymology: A modern American coinage close to Zaire and Zyaire. Zaire, the former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, comes from a Kikongo word for 'river'.
An English surname from Raydon in Suffolk, but in the US mostly a modern blend of Ray and the -ayden sound of Jayden and Brayden. It overlaps with Raiden, the Japanese thunder god.

assoc.t: Raiden (also Rayden), thunder god of Mortal Kombat

e.etymology: From trey, the word for a three in cards and dice, from Old French treis. It began as a nickname for a boy who is the third of his name (III) and became a given name in the late 20th century.
namesakes: Trey Parker (co-creator of South Park)
Trey Songz (R&B singer)
Trey Anastasio (Phish frontman)

assoc.t: trey, a three-pointer in basketball

e.etymology: From Hebrew avi, 'my father', mostly a short form of Avraham (Abraham) and Avner. It is common in Israel and in American Jewish families.

e.meaning: one who lives or works by a bridge
e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived by or kept a bridge. In the American West it recalls mountain man Jim Bridger, whose name marks mountains, forests and towns in Montana and Wyoming.

assoc.t: Jim Bridger, frontier mountain man and scout

e.etymology: A modern name with several possible sources, including a short form of Anaya and a spelling of Naia. Actress Naya Rivera of Glee made it familiar in the US from 2009.
namesakes: Naya Rivera (actress, Santana on Glee)

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that swaps a Z into the pattern of Kaylee, Jaylee and Baylee.
From an English surname and place name, a spelling of Berkeley, Old English beorc and leah, 'birch wood or clearing'.

assoc.t: Berkeley, California, and its university
Berkley, fishing tackle brand
Berklee College of Music in Boston

e.etymology: From the English word mercy, taken up as a virtue name by 17th-century Puritans. The word comes through French from Latin merces, 'reward', later 'pity'. It can also anglicize Mercedes.

assoc.t: Mercy, name of many Catholic hospitals
Mercy, healer hero in the video game Overwatch

e.etymology: The feminine of Paul, from the Roman family name Paulus, 'small' or 'humble'. Saint Paula was a 4th-century Roman noblewoman who worked with Saint Jerome.
namesakes: Paula Abdul (singer and American Idol judge)
Paula Deen (Southern TV chef)
Paula Patton (actress)

e.etymology: The English word for a bright flame, used as a name, and also a spelling of Blaise, the French saint's name from Latin Blasius, traditionally read as 'lisping'.

assoc.t: blaze, the everyday word for a fire
Blaze and the Monster Machines, Nick Jr. cartoon truck
Blaze Pizza, fast-casual pizza chain
blaze, slang for smoking marijuana

e.etymology: The feminine of Milan, from the Slavic root mil, meaning dear, kind or gracious. Common in Russia and the Balkans; in the US it also reads as a longer form of Mila.
namesakes: Milana Vayntrub (actress who plays Lily in AT&T commercials)

e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived by a ridge, from Middle English rigg and Old Norse hryggr. Its use as a first name is recent.
namesakes: Martin Riggs (Mel Gibson's detective in Lethal Weapon)
Bobby Riggs (tennis champion of the Battle of the Sexes match)

assoc.t: Martin Riggs, Mel Gibson's cop in Lethal Weapon

e.meaning: from Lassy, a town in Normandy
e.etymology: From a Norman surname taken from Lassy in Calvados, France. A boys' name in the 1800s, it became a girls' name in the 1970s, helped by its echo of the word lace.
namesakes: Lacey Chabert (actress in Mean Girls and Hallmark films)

e.meaning: traditionally exalted or mountain of strength
e.etymology: A spelling of Aaron, the Hebrew name of Moses's brother in the Bible; its original meaning is uncertain. Aron is the standard form in Scandinavia, Poland and Hungary.
namesakes: Aron Ralston (hiker whose ordeal became the film 127 Hours)
